documents.title: Setting up a Signup Form - Forms - Documentation - Carrd
Carrd - Simple, free, fully responsive one-page sites for pretty much anything

segments: A freelance designer or illustrator whose entire web presence is a link-in-bio page, now pitching work to clients who ask for a website
Someone launching a small thing — a newsletter, a waitlist, a course, an album — who needs a page that captures emails into the list tool they already pay for, before launch day
A technical freelancer or small studio who has built a few free Carrd pages for clients and has just run out of sites
gaps: No customer names, quotes or case studies found - the copy can describe the product but cannot prove anyone uses it
No measurable results found - emails may describe documented capabilities but cannot invent measured outcomes

business.what_it_does: Lets anyone build a simple, fully responsive one-page site from a template or blank page and publish it.
business.business_model: freemium subscription (free tier plus paid Pro plans billed per year)

facts.statement: Carrd is described as "Simple, free, fully responsive one-page sites for pretty much anything."

provenance.quote: Simple, free, fully responsive one-page sites for pretty much anything.

facts.statement: A free account can build up to three sites and use all of Carrd's core features.

provenance.quote: Build up to three sites per account and use all of Carrd's core features – for free!

facts.statement: Starting a Pro trial requires no payment or credit card.

provenance.quote: Test drive Pro's top features (like custom domains and advanced forms) free for a full 7 days – no payment or credit card required.

facts.statement: Signup forms (capturing visitor names/emails to services like Mailchimp, Kit, ActiveCampaign, HubSpot, Klaviyo, etc.) require Pro Standard or higher.
Carrd launched a native, cookie-free site analytics service called Carrd Analytics in October 2026.

provenance.quote: Launched Carrd Analytics, our native, cookie-free site analytics service that requires minimal setup and provides reporting directly within the dashboard

facts.statement: Higher Pro plans raise the site limit beyond the free tier's three sites, up to 25 sites on a Plus plan.

provenance.quote: Build and publish more than three sites from a single Carrd account – from 10 sites on a Standard plan to 25 sites on a Plus plan (and beyond).

facts.statement: Carrd supports contact, signup, custom, and payment-enabled forms as a feature set.

provenance.quote: Add contact, signup (using Mailchimp, Kit, ActiveCampaign, EmailOctopus, and many more), custom, and payment-enabled forms.

facts.statement: Carrd is used mainly for lightweight personal, landing, portfolio, and showcase-style sites rather than complex multi-page sites.

provenance.quote: This is the entry-level Pro plan. At just $9 / year, it offers some nice improvements over the free Basic experience while still being extremely affordable.

This is the mid-tier Pro plan. At $19 / year, this is by far the most popular Pro plan in part because it covers a wide range of use cases: from individuals further branding their sites with custom domains to businesses using forms to collect email

This is the top-tier Pro plan. At $49 / year, this plan is built for power users as it offers not only the features of Pro Standard, but also more powerful, developer-friendly features like custom forms, the advanced settings

voice.tone: Plain, friendly, reassuring — explains things in everyday words, admits uncertainty ('usually', 'sometimes') instead of overpromising, and leans on parentheticals to add a human aside rather than a formal caveat.
voice.rhythm: Short, direct sentences strung together with commas and dashes; one idea per sentence, with asides tucked into parentheses rather than subordinate clauses.
voice.person: We — speaks as a small team to 'you', never a named individual, no bylines or signatures.
exemplars: Have a question or need help with something? Check out the **[documentation](/docs)**, or simply use the form below to get in touch. If you have a copyright issue you'd like to report, please use [this form](/contact/copyright) instead.
Note: We *usually* reply within 24 hours (sometimes a lot sooner), but if you don't hear from us please check your spam/junk folder *or* reach out again from an alternate email.

Welcome to the official Carrd documentation! We've tried to provide answers and instructions for the most common questions and tasks, but if you can't find what you're looking for here please [get in touch](/contact).

Test drive Pro's top features (like custom domains and advanced forms) free for a full **7 days** – no payment or credit card required. Upgrade to a full Pro plan at any time during or after your trial.

segments.name: A freelance designer or illustrator whose entire web presence is a link-in-bio page, now pitching work to clients who ask for a website
segments.situation: Inferred, not observed: their work lives on Instagram, Behance or a Notion page, and when a prospect asks "do you have a site?" the answer is a handle. They have probably started and abandoned something heavier — a WordPress install, a Squarespace trial, a half-built Webflow project — because a portfolio one-pager did not justify a CMS, a theme and a monthly bill. What they need is a single page with their name on it, their own domain, and nothing in the footer that reads as a free tool. Carrd's own framing of who pays at $19/year is "individuals further branding their sites with custom domains", which matches this reader; the abandoned-tool history is a hypothesis, not something the supplied material documents.

At **$19** / year, this is by far the most popular Pro plan in part because it covers a wide range of use cases: from individuals further branding their sites with [custom domains](/docs/sites/using-a-custom-domain) to businesses using forms to collect email addresses and [customer feedback](/docs/forms/setting-up-a-contact-form).

segments.job_to_be_done: Be taken seriously as a professional when someone looks them up — have a place to send people that looks like they own it, without becoming a part-time webmaster.
segments.trigger: A prospect, gallery, recruiter or collaborator asks for a link and the only thing to send is a social profile — or they buy a domain for their name and have nowhere to point it.

pains.statement: Carrd names this buyer's motive itself: individuals paying the mid-tier plan to further brand their sites with custom domains.

pains.statement: Hypothesis, not observed buyer behaviour: a free-tier footer credit and a builder-branded URL are the details this reader expects a client to notice, so the page they are proud of is the one thing they hesitate to send.
Hypothesis: every full site builder they have tried asked them to make decisions they do not have opinions about — templates, page trees, plugins, hosting — for a site that is one screen long.
Hypothesis: they own a domain, or will buy one, and expect DNS and SSL to be the part that defeats them.

segments.name: Someone launching a small thing — a newsletter, a waitlist, a course, an album — who needs a page that captures emails into the list tool they already pay for, before launch day
segments.situation: Inferred, not observed: there is a date. Something ships, opens or goes on sale, and between now and then they need a page that does one job: take a name and an email and put it where their list already lives (Mailchimp, Kit, ConvertKit-style tooling, beehiiv, Klaviyo). They are not short of places to build a page; they are short of a page that reliably posts to their list without an embed script they have to debug. Carrd's own description of the mid-tier buyer includes "businesses using forms to collect email addresses and customer feedback". Worth knowing for the copy: signup forms are gated — a free account can build and publish the page but cannot wire up the signup form, which is the part this reader came for.
segments.job_to_be_done: Have an audience to talk to on launch day instead of launching into silence — start collecting names now, with the page done this evening rather than this month.
segments.trigger: A launch or open date lands in the calendar, or they finish setting up an email tool and realise they have no page pointing at it. Also: an existing page's embedded form breaks or starts dropping signups.

pains.statement: Carrd describes this buyer directly: businesses on the $19/year plan using forms to collect email addresses and customer feedback.

pains.statement: Documented constraint this reader will hit: the signup form — the reason they are building the page — requires Pro Standard or higher, so the free build stops one step short of working.
Hypothesis, not observed: the deadline is the real pressure. A builder that needs a weekend of learning is disqualified no matter how good the output.
Hypothesis: they have already chosen their email tool and will not switch it to suit a page builder, so an integration list that omits their provider ends the evaluation.

segments.name: A technical freelancer or small studio who has built a few free Carrd pages for clients and has just run out of sites
segments.situation: Inferred, not observed: they discovered Carrd for their own page, then used it for a client who needed a landing page by Friday, and now there are three. The fourth client is waiting. The things they want next are the things a developer wants: their own code and script tags on the page, form submissions going somewhere other than an inbox (Zapier, Make, Airtable, a URL), a password on a staging page before the client approves it, and the sources downloadable in case the relationship or the tool changes. Carrd positions its top tier for exactly this reader — "built for power users" with "developer-friendly features" — and also speaks to people moving existing sites in. Whether this reader actually resells client work on Carrd is a hypothesis; the supplied material documents the capabilities, not the practice.

objections.objection: "The free tier already does what I need — three sites and all the core features. Why would I pay anything?"
objections.answer: Concede it: the free tier really is three sites plus core features, so the honest paid case is a short list of specific gates, not "more". The things you cannot do free are: point your own domain at the page with SSL, wire a signup form to your email tool, drop the "Made with Carrd" footer, and use a premium URL. If none of those four matter this month, free is the right answer and the copy should not pretend otherwise. Note the trap for the $9 tier: Pro Lite still caps at three sites, so "more sites" is not what Lite buys.

objections.objection: "One page is not a website. I need a blog, a services page, a case-study section — a real multi-page site."
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence answers this. Every documented capability is scoped to one-page sites; the closest thing is redirecting "slash" URLs to sections of the same page, which is navigation inside one page, not multiple pages. There is no evidence of multi-page sites, a blog or a CMS. This objection cannot be beaten with what we know — the only honest move is to disqualify this reader early rather than imply otherwise.

objections.objection: "I'd have to deal with DNS records and an SSL certificate. That's the part where I give up and the site sits broken for a week."
objections.answer: SSL is not a thing they configure: custom domains come with full SSL support via Let's Encrypt, and there is a documented, step-by-step path for both using a custom domain and setting up SSL. A custom subdomain is also supported if they would rather not touch the apex record. What the evidence does not do is quantify how long propagation takes or promise it is painless, so do not claim "two minutes".

objections.objection: "It's a tiny product on a yearly plan. If it shuts down or jacks up the price, my site and my client's site vanish and I have nothing to move."
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and the limits matter. Pro Plus lets you download the unminified HTML, CSS, JS and images for any site you build — but it explicitly excludes server-side code, which means the forms do not come with you, and that exit hatch only exists at $49/year, not at $9 or $19. There is also nothing in the evidence about company size, funding, uptime or longevity, so any reassurance beyond "you can download the front end on the top plan" is unsupported.

objections.objection: "Clients and customers can tell a page was made with a cheap builder. I'd rather have nothing than look amateur."
objections.answer: Four specific tells get removed on Pro: the "Made with Carrd" footer branding goes, the page sits on a domain you own with SSL (or an unbranded premium URL like .crd.co), the address bar shows your favicon, and shared links show a custom image instead of an automatic screenshot. Premium starting-point templates are Pro-only. All of this is capability evidence from Carrd's own docs — there is no independent or customer evidence about how the output is perceived, so the copy can promise the tells are gone and must not promise anyone was impressed.

objections.objection: "Cheap builders never integrate with the email tool I actually use, so the signups end up stuck in a form I have to export by hand."
objections.answer: This one is answerable by name, which is the strongest card in the whole deck. Signup forms capture visitor names and emails into twenty named destinations — ActiveCampaign, beehiiv, Brevo, Buttondown, EmailOctopus, GetResponse, Ghost, HubSpot, Kit, Klaviyo, Loops, Mailchimp, MailerLite, Mailjet, Omnisend, Resend, Sender, SendFox, SendGrid, Sendy. Say the reader's provider out loud. The condition to state plainly: this needs Pro Standard or higher. For anything not on the list, Pro Plus custom forms can post to Zapier, Make, n8n, Airtable or a URL.

objections.objection: "I could build this myself in an afternoon with plain HTML and host it free on GitHub Pages or Netlify."
objections.answer: Not beatable on principle with the evidence we have — and for a technical reader it is true. What the evidence offers is the parts they would otherwise hand-roll and maintain: hosted forms with spam protection and Stripe payments, SSL via Let's Encrypt, password protection, advanced element settings, your own script tags and embeds, and the unminified sources if you want to take the page and leave. There is no evidence about time saved, so do not assert it; the only argument available is "these specific pieces already exist and are included".

objections.objection: "No refund, no money-back guarantee — I'm paying a year up front for something I haven't used."
objections.answer: There is no guarantee in the evidence; none was found. What substitutes is testing before paying: a 7-day trial of Pro's top features, including custom domains and advanced forms, with no payment and no credit card required, and you can upgrade during or after it. Separately, you can start building with no signup at all, so the page can exist before any account does. Auto-renewal is a documented action you take, not something the evidence shows as default. One honest wrinkle: the homepage version of the trial pitch mentions that PayPal and major cards are accepted, so the copy should state the no-card condition using the /pro wording rather than implying cards are never requested anywhere.

objections.objection: "This is not for a team — there are no seats, no roles, and I can't hand a site to a client or a colleague without giving away my login."
objections.answer: Half answered. You can share access to your sites with other Carrd users and transfer ownership of a site to another user, both from Pro Lite upward, and sites can be organised into custom folders or archived. That covers handover. What the evidence does not contain is anything about seats, roles, permissions levels or team billing — so if the reader means "my agency needs five people in one account", nothing here resolves it.

objections.objection: "At $19 a year there is no support. When something breaks before a launch I'll be shouting into a contact form."
objections.answer: Weakly answered, and the hedge has to be kept. Carrd says it *usually* replies within 24 hours, sometimes sooner — explicitly typical, not a committed response time — and the only channel in evidence is a contact form, alongside documentation. There is no SLA, no live chat and no priority support for higher plans in the evidence. Quote the hedge rather than rounding it to "24-hour support".

objections.objection: "I'll have no idea whether the page is working, and I don't want to bolt on Google Analytics and then owe a cookie banner."
objections.answer: Carrd Analytics launched on 2 October 2026 as a native, cookie-free analytics service with minimal setup and reporting inside the dashboard; third-party providers like Google Analytics, Plausible and Matomo remain optional. Pages can also collect UTM parameter values. Available on Pro Standard and Pro Plus. Two cautions: "cookie-free" is Carrd's description of its own service and is not a legal opinion, and nothing in the evidence dates it as novel relative to competitors.

objections.objection: "I already have a Linktree / Notion page / Instagram bio doing this job. Moving means breaking links people have already saved."
objections.answer: Only partly answered, and only on the top plan. Carrd speaks directly to people moving sites in and offers redirects to preserve existing links by sending them to sections or external URLs — but redirects sit in Pro Plus at $49/year, and canonical URL control does too. Nothing in the evidence addresses migrating from a link-in-bio service specifically, importing content, or keeping an old URL alive, so the switching cost is real and should be acknowledged rather than waved away.
